# Final Summary
The Norway Scholarship, established in 1919 by Arthur Ivor Garland Jayne, facilitates Norwegian studies at Wadham College, Oxford. Funded by an initial donation of NOK 60,000 and a 1978 campaign raising NOK 1.17 million, the program—now overseen by a committee of Oxford alumni and the Norwegian Ambassador—has awarded degrees across diverse fields since 1920. Notable recipients include Trygve Leivestad, Just Faaland, and Bjørnar Sverdrup-Thygeson, although awards were suspended during World War II and other specific periods.
In contrast, the Kennedy Scholarship, created in 1964 by Prime Minister Alec Douglas-Home following the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, serves as a living memorial for UK citizens to study at Harvard or MIT. Managed by a Trust appointed by the UK Prime Minister, which includes former scholars and US university representatives, the selection process is a rigorous national competition evaluating intellectual attainment, public service potential, and personal resilience. Since its inception, nearly 600 scholars have been awarded, including prominent figures such as Ed Balls, Yvette Cooper, and David Miliband.
The scholarship has produced a distinguished list of notable scholars across multiple fields, including Economics and Finance (featuring former Bank of England Governor Mervyn King and economist Charlotte Hogg), Journalism (with contributors like Zanny Minton Beddoes and Simon Kuper), Arts (including poet Hannah Sullivan), and Academia (encompassing figures such as philosopher Gareth Evans and historian Rana Mitter). Additionally, the program recognizes prominent legal experts, including Supreme Court Justices Mary Arden and Nicholas Hamblen, highlighting its success in fostering high-level expertise in diverse disciplines.
